title: Jasur's Summer at the Bazaar
intro: You are going to read about a teenager from Samarkand who got his first job and learned how to save money.

passage: Last summer, sixteen-year-old Jasur got his first job. He worked at his uncle's fruit stall in Siyob Bazaar, the biggest market in Samarkand. "I wanted a new laptop for school, but it cost five million som," he says. "My parents said, 'Good idea. But you can earn the money yourself.'"

Jasur started work at six o'clock in the morning, six days a week. First he carried heavy boxes of peaches and grapes from the truck. Then he washed the fruit and put it on the table in neat lines. At seven, the first customers arrived. Many of them wanted to bargain. "The grandmothers were the best at it," Jasur laughs. "They always got a lower price than everyone else!"

His uncle paid him a wage of 80,000 som a day, in cash. On the first day, Jasur put the money in his wallet and felt very rich. But by the evening, he spent half of it on ice cream, a phone card and a taxi home. "That was a big mistake," he says. "I worked for ten hours and spent the money in thirty minutes."

That night, his older sister helped him make a budget. They wrote it in a small notebook. Every day, Jasur kept 10,000 som for lunch and the bus, and he put the rest in a tin box under his bed. He also wrote his goal on the first page: "Laptop by September!" Before he wanted to spend money on something, he looked at that page and asked, "Do I really need this?"

After ten weeks, Jasur counted his money. He had more than four million som. That was still not enough to afford the laptop, but his parents were proud of his hard work and paid the rest. Jasur still saves a little money every week. "The laptop is great," he says, "but the best thing I got from the bazaar is a new habit."
